tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

## After the landing: the coordinator's routing

The coordinator's steps after a landing, in this order, each done whole:

1. The landing report to the curator.
   1a. The base build of the landed tree, and F-34's measure on it. The base build is a worktree at the landing commit, outside the main tree, built as "Before the launch", step 2, gives it, and then left alone. The measure runs in a scratch worktree seeded from it (`tools/seed-worktree.sh <the base build> <scratch> - <landing>`): `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/planner/codegen-measure.sh <scratch-worktree> <out-dir>` applies its patch to the worktree it is given and builds it, so it is never given the main tree or a base build (its header), about 60 s for the build and 160 s for the probe on an idle machine. Its table, its list and the comparison with F-34's last figure, declaration by declaration, are committed in one file under the batch plan's `probes/` folder, `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-<N>/probes/measure-<landing>.txt`; the scratch worktree is then removed (`git -C /home/user/fortress worktree remove --force <scratch>`, since the patch leaves it edited), and F-34 takes the figure in step 3. Through climb batch 33's run 1 no stage owned the measure after a landing (`reviews/batch-33-review.md`, process finding 2); after 33b the coordinator's worker took it twelve minutes after the push, on the brief of the day (`3fbce96856`, `compile-ladder/plan-33/probes/measure-ba3c7c876d.txt`; `reviews/batch-33b-review.md`, process finding 2).
2. The routing: every open row, record default and item for the curator filed with a batch or as a parked line of `PLAN.md`. Each is checked against POSITIONS and the notes `INDEX.md` lists before it is called open, put to the curator or briefed. In the same pass the routing moves out of `PLAN.md` each item the batch built or answered, and any item it finds stale: word for word, into `PLAN-history.md`, under the landing's dated heading and the heading the item stood under. The batch's own line in its phase becomes one line, with its landing commit and its review. An open item whose text also stands in another home (a `review-queue.md` entry, a ledger row, a FACTS or POSITIONS entry) becomes one line in `PLAN.md`: what is asked, its default, and a pointer to that home. No other step takes an item out of `PLAN.md`, which held 519K characters before its consolidation of 2026-10-15, 54 % of them closed (`process-engineering/plan-map.md`, sections 2 and 4).
3. FACTS consolidated as its README says, superseded text moved to `FACTS-history.md`. The commit stage has already written the landed count and distance, and the two stages' seconds (F-53, F-240).

   - One task for the standing skill writer (`tools/skill-writer.sh`, its brief `skill-writer-brief.md`): the batch's revival-change material, the section "Revival changes, for the skill writer" of its `RECORD.md`; the skill sentences that the post-batch review lists as false; and any `skill-touched` item. The writer runs `tools/skills-lint.py` before each commit.
   - A cold read of the parts the writer changed, by an agent given only the skill and `skill-cold-read-brief.md`.
   - The writer fixes the cold read's flags, and the coordinator pushes its commits.
5. The next batch launched only after that, so that its workers read the updated skill (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The landing").

"""plan-moves.py --root WT --base AT [--stale-at REV]: check that every line taken out of PLAN.md went to PLAN-history.md word for word, and list the PLAN lines that look stale.

A line taken out is a line of PLAN.md at AT, the commit that the worktree WT was made at, that the working
PLAN.md no longer holds, as a whole line: a line moved, cut to a pointer, or changed. Each must stand among
the lines that the working PLAN-history.md gained since AT, as many times as it went. PLAN-history.md only
gains: a line that it lost is a failure too. Blank lines are not counted. Prints the counts, the headings
that PLAN-history.md gained, and each failure; exit 1 on any.

Then, for information only (they never fail), the PLAN lines to look at, one `LOOK` line each with its
reason, read against the working review queue and the history of AT:
  settled   a list line whose own pointer, a sentence "Review-queue item 296.", names items that are each
            settled in the queue's part (a), and that names no item open in (b) or (c); it skips a line that
            already carries a cleanup's mark, "closed at the cleanup of DATE" in any of the queue cleanup's
            forms ("(closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05: learning)", "item 127, closed at the cleanup of
            2026-11-05: settled", "are closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05 (learning)"): the cleanup marked
            it in place, and moving it out of PLAN is PLAN's consolidation, not a landing's change
  list      a list line that names three or more items, some of them settled; or one that ties its items
            to a list of the queue's head (the queue's "Needed before the switch-over") and does not name
            the same items
  finding   a line `- Climb batch N's review, finding M ...` whose finding a commit in the history of AT
            names (`batch-N-review.md, finding M`, or "climb batch N's finding M"), where that commit
            changes a file outside the record: a half of the line may be built
With --stale-at REV, it reads PLAN.md and the review queue at REV, and the history of REV, prints only the
LOOK lines, and exits 0: evidence.py gives them to the sorter in plan.md.

"""plan-moves.py --root WT --base AT [--stale-at REV]: check that every line taken out of PLAN.md went to PLAN-history.md word for word, and list the PLAN lines that look stale.

A line taken out is a line of PLAN.md at AT, the commit that the worktree WT was made at, that the working
PLAN.md no longer holds, as a whole line: a line moved, cut to a pointer, or changed. Each must stand among
the lines that the working PLAN-history.md gained since AT, as many times as it went. PLAN-history.md only
gains: a line that it lost is a failure too. Blank lines are not counted. Prints the counts, the headings
that PLAN-history.md gained, and each failure; exit 1 on any.

Then, for information only (they never fail), the PLAN lines to look at, one `LOOK` line each with its
reason, read against the working review queue and the history of AT:
  settled   a list line whose own pointer, a sentence "Review-queue item 296.", names items that are each

            already carries a cleanup's mark, "closed at the cleanup of DATE" in any of the queue cleanup's
            forms ("(closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05: learning)", "item 127, closed at the cleanup of
            2026-11-05: settled", "are closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05 (learning)"): the cleanup marked

  list      a list line that names three or more items, some of them settled; or one that ties its items

  finding   a line `- Climb batch N's review, finding M ...` whose finding a commit in the history of AT

            changes a file outside the record: a half of the line may be built
With --stale-at REV, it reads PLAN.md and the review queue at REV, and the history of REV, prints only the
LOOK lines, and exits 0: evidence.py gives them to the sorter in plan.md.

launches with two different class paths, and nothing in `Shell.java` knows
about `run` (`modules-and-phases.md` B.0).

**`Shell` picks a world and a phase order.** `Shell.subMain` is one `if`-chain
over the subcommand (`Shell.java:395-516`). Each arm sets three things: which
**prelude** the run links against (the library a program gets without importing
it), whether the type checker runs, and which list of phases to build. For

are two arrays in one file (`phases/PhaseOrder.java:125-147`).

`FortressBuiltin` + `AnyType` for the interpreter, `CompilerLibrary` +
`CompilerBuiltin` + `AnyType` for the compiler
(`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:113-137`).

with holes in it (section 2); in code generation, the single class emitted for

unrelated.

## 6. The run: the second JVM and the class loader

**The second JVM.** `bin/fortress run` hands off to `bin/run`, which launches
`com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper` (`bin/fortress:16-18`,
`bin/run:41`). The class path puts `bytecode_cache`, `bytecode_cache/*` and
`nativewrapper_cache` **ahead** of the tool class path
(`bin/run_classpath:26`).

**The trap in that ordering.** If the library jars are not in
`bytecode_cache`, the loader silently falls back to frozen stubs compiled from
checked-in Java sources into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/` — an older
snapshot of `CompilerBuiltin` — and the program dies with a
`NoSuchMethodError` on a method that plainly exists in the `.fss`
(`repo-internals.md:162-182`; `modules-and-phases.md` B.13). The cure is to
compile the five library components in order first; the recipe is in
`repo-internals.md:170-180`. This is a cache problem misread as a compiler bug
for years (`repo-internals.md:152-160`).

**What `MainWrapper` does.** It first stashes the program's arguments in a
static field rather than passing them. It then initializes the named component's
class, and the class of each component that it uses, through
`InstantiatingClassloader.ONLY`, in a root task (F-348). Then it invokes the
named class's no-argument `main` (`runtimeSystem/MainWrapper.java:19, 30-46,
94-98`, at climb batch 30's landing, `d89fc0fda4`).

**The class loader is where compiled Fortress stops being ordinary bytecode.**
`InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` (2,946 lines in the file; the method at
`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178`) examines the class *name*
for markers and, for most of them, **generates** the class instead of reading
it (`:227-296`):

- a tuple RTTI class, an arrow RTTI class (`:227-232`);
- a generic function instance, by reading the template and rewriting it
  (`:233-242`);
- a closure (`:243-244`);
- for a name in oxford or angle brackets: arrow interfaces and their abstract
  and wrapped forms, tuple types, concrete and "any" tuples, union types, and —
  the general case — an instantiation of a generic template
  (`:245-280`);
- an RTTI class, translated to flush out symbolic references (`:281-290`);
